preamble: Pharyngealization (emphaticization) of plain [s] to the emphatic [sˤ], Arabic ṣād ص. The documented cases are loanwords in Arabic, in which Italian, French and English s is taken over as ṣ in words such as these: Italian sala > صالة, French salon > صالون /sˤaː.luːn/, English bus > باص [bɑːsˤ]. The adaptation is not uniform: Egyptian أسانسير 'elevator', from French ascenseur, is given both with plain /ʔa.san.seːr/ and with emphatic /ʔa.sˤan.sˤeːr/. Wiktionary gives صِرَاط ṣirāṭ 'path' as a variant of سِرَاط sirāṭ, borrowed from Syriac ˀesṭrāṭ (itself from Latin strāta), so that older loan has both s and ṣ. Arabic قَصْر qaṣr 'castle' is not counted: its ṣ was already in the Aramaic source qaṣrā (Wiktionary). The reverse change, loss of emphasis in Maltese and Cypriot Arabic, is filed under [sˤ] > [s].

examples.to: Arabic صالة 'hall, large room', South Levantine ṣāle [ˈsˤɑː.le]
Arabic صالون /sˤaː.luːn/ 'reception hall, salon', Moroccan ṣālūn 'living room'

examples.note: Wiktionary also gives /ʔa.san.seːr/ with plain s.

examples.to: Arabic باص bāṣ 'bus', Gulf (Kuwait) /bɑːsˤ/, South Levantine [bɑːsˤ]

examples.note: Wiktionary gives both English and French soda as the source.
